Salamanca
sal-uh-MANG-kuh
n. (the Castilian university city whose theological school argued the rights of the American Indians and whose Hebraist Luis de Leon was imprisoned by the Inquisition)
From Latin Salmantica, a Vettones town on the Tormes, of pre-Roman origin.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Salamanca held the oldest university in Spain, chartered in 1218, and in the sixteenth century the most important faculty of theology in Catholic Europe. Francisco de Vitoria, holding the prime chair from 1526, delivered the lectures on the Indies which argued that the American peoples were true owners of their lands, that neither papal grant nor imperial title conferred a right of conquest, that unbelief forfeits no property, and that a war of conquest for religion is unjust; from that root grew the modern law of nations. Domingo de Soto, Melchor Cano and later Francisco Suarez continued the school. Salamanca also tried its own: Luis de Leon, Augustinian and Hebraist, was imprisoned by the Inquisition from 1572 to 1576 for preferring the Hebrew text to the Vulgate and for translating the Song of Songs into Spanish, and resumed his chair with the remark that he had been saying when interrupted. The dictionary records Salamanca as proof that conscience survived in the Spanish church, and that it was punished there.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a chair as a professorship; conquest as the subjection of a country by force; dominion as the right of possession and use; Hebraist is not in Webster, but Hebrew is the language of the Hebrews; and conscience as the internal judge of right and wrong.

expand to see more

CHAIR, n. A seat of justice or of authority; a professorship in a university or college.

CONQUEST, n. The act of conquering; the subjection of a country or people by war or force; that which is conquered.

DOMINION, n. Sovereign authority; the power of governing; the territory under a government; right of possession and use.

HEBREW, n. A Jew; one of the descendants of Abraham; the language of the Hebrews.

CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty which decides on the lawfulness of our own actions.

Key Scripture

Pro 31:9 — "Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy."

Pro 22:22 — "Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate:"

Isa 1:17 — "Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow."

Mic 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Modern Corruption

Castilian university city of Vitoria's lectures on the rights of the American Indians and of Luis de Leon's imprisonment for preferring the Hebrew text.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the theology of conquest, and the honour belongs here to the men who refused it from inside the conquering church. Vitoria taught at the height of Spanish power that heathen nations own their land, that the pope cannot grant what is not his, and that no war for the faith is just. He was not a Protestant and he was not disciplined; he was simply right, and he reasoned from the law that protects the weak against the strong: “Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate” (Pro 22:22).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that the defence of the defenceless is an office and not a sentiment. Solomon gives it to the king as a duty of speech, “Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy” (Pro 31:9), and Isaiah lists the acts that constitute a reformed nation: “relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isa 1:17). The whole requirement is three clauses long, “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8), and the dictionary observes that the same university which produced that teaching also imprisoned a man for reading Hebrew. A faculty may be braver about distant injustice than about the tribunal down the street.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dal (H1800), poor; Hebrew din (H1777), to plead a cause; Hebrew mishpat (H4941), justice.

expand to see more

Hebrew dal (H1800) — low, weak, poor; “Rob not the poor, because he is poor”, Proverbs 22:22.

Hebrew 'ani (H6041) — afflicted, humble, needy; “neither oppress the afflicted in the gate”, Proverbs 22:22.

Hebrew din (H1777) — to judge, to plead a cause; “and plead the cause of the poor and needy”, Proverbs 31:9.

Hebrew shaphat (H8199) — to judge, to govern; “judge the fatherless, plead for the widow”, Isaiah 1:17.

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice; “to do justly, and to love mercy”, Micah 6:8.

Usage

"“Rob not the poor, because he is poor” (Pro 22:22) — the law Vitoria reasoned from."

"“and plead the cause of the poor and needy” (Pro 31:9) — defence of the defenceless as an office."

"“relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isa 1:17) — what constitutes a reformed nation."
